extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and practitioners interested in science, education, librarianship, and natural history (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and informal standards for reviewing and producing popular-science, educational, and natural-history publications (including book notices, institutional circulars, field guides, and short scientific reports). Emphasizes audience-appropriateness, clarity, documentation, illustrative material, and methodological transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriateness for children's astronomy primers
rubrics_metrics.description: The immature mind cannot grasp the order of ideas involved in astronomical relations; primers hitherto made for the purpose are failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting abstract astronomical truths that require mature comprehension; do not substitute mere verbal acquisition for real understanding. While children can learn astronomical words, teaching complex concepts they cannot seize is unsuitable for education and leads to the 'bane of education' — learning words without knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and content balance for history books for young readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Presented in an easy, flowing style designed to engage and hold the interest of young readers; important events given in fuller detail than usual, though stories are not told simply because interesting, and much that would be burdensome to memory is omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for engaging prose, fuller treatment of significant events, and omit material merely burdensome to memory; when revising for a different national audience (e.g., American students), state and justify the nature and necessity of revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library-building design principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Object is not to formulate rules that must be rigidly followed, but to set forth the conditions for library-buildings which experience has shown to be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance should be practical and experience-based rather than strictly prescriptive; emphasize indispensable conditions (lighting, ventilation, layout, etc.) derived from librarian experience instead of inflexible rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-guide / collector's manual design for amateurs
rubrics_metrics.description: A book intended as a real and helpful guide to those who, though not expert botanists and using only a simple pocket magnifier, desire to begin the collection and study of marine plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make guides accessible to non-experts: include clear practical directions, suitable for users with minimal equipment; assist preparation with input from adepts and provide ample illustrations to aid identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: State survey / agricultural report accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: This report is designed for the information of the general public, as well as of the statistician and student, and is therefore thrown into a popular form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing state surveys, consider popular use of results; present technical findings in a form accessible to general readers to increase public support, sustainment, and completeness of future surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic design for eye hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the several letters, particularly those which are allied in form, as distinct as possible; favor fashions in type-cutting that accentuate distinctions. The superior importance of the upper part of the letters is enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize distinct letterforms (especially upper curves); avoid strokes so thick they blur letters; ensure members of easily-confused groups (a, c, e, o, s) are more clearly distinguished; long letters usually rise above the line rather than fall below; only young readers require particularly heavy strokes; prefer typecuts that improve discrimination and thus reduce eye strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation method for the center of population
rubrics_metrics.description: The center is defined as the point at which equilibrium would be reached if the country were a plane surface loaded with its inhabitants (the center of gravity of the population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find the center approximately by assuming a point and computing north/south and east/west moments (aggregate products of local populations by distances from assumed parallels/meridians). Treat large cities as special centers; group remaining population by square degrees (centers of those squares as local centers). Account for map projection distortions and the spheroidal shape of the earth; expect approximate results and apply iterative corrections from moment differences divided by total population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitation assessment criteria for cemeteries
rubrics_metrics.description: A commission was to inquire whether sanitation could be accomplished by chemical or physical agents combined with drainage; whether disappearance of organic parts of bodies could be expedited by additions in coffins or soil; and whether such additions were likely to do any harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings reported: gases from corpses buried at 1.5 m (five feet) do not reach the surface; nearly the entire organic constituents of bodies are consumed in about five years; drainage accelerates consumption; open-air cemeteries are not generally dangerous; wells are safe if at reasonable distance. However, these conclusions may be modified by later research on cadaveric alkaloids (ptomaines) and on preservation of pathogens (e.g., Pasteur's findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for archaeological site reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume gives history of the Pueblos, the theories urged, and the results of examinations, surveys, and measurements of the ruins with views, plans, sections, and estimates, and observations as appropriate concerning the character, customs, and arts of the Indians who constructed the buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archaeological reports should combine historical context and theory with careful field results: measured surveys, plans and sections, illustrations (views, plates), estimates, and culturally informed observations about builders' character and arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for short observational scientific reports (eclipse example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Langley's observations reported narrow, structureless ring of vivid light, a nebulous luminosity extending around, a stream of light with parallel borders, and coarse filamentary structure in the corona; assistants observed color-phenomena in clouds during totality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short observational reports should record the most interesting observable features in precise descriptive terms, include plates/illustrations where possible, and note unusual transient phenomena (e.g., color effects in clouds) observed by different observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard in antiquity/prehistorical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases of human relics found in California assigned pre-glacial antiquity may not require that conclusion; nothing in situation or condition of the relics makes a post-glacial origin impossible or improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming great antiquity from isolated finds; weigh situational and condition evidence carefully and consider alternative, more recent origins before asserting pre-glacial antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical standard for assessing philosophical/ethical essays
rubrics_metrics.description: An essay opposing materialism of forty-three pages in large type is described as a very commonplace argument, slight in quality and form, that 'can help nobody.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate essays for originality, depth, and practical usefulness; mere restatement without substantive argument or new insight is grounds for unfavorable assessment.
